To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a high-fat, high-cholesterol (HFHC) diet robustly alters miRNA expression in mouse liver and that we have identified a module of co-regulated liver miRNAs significantly correlated with circulating low-density lipid cholesterol (LDLc) in the Diversity Outbred mouse.
we identified a co-regulated network of miRNAs that are associated with plasma LDL-C in a mouse model of diet-induced dyslipidaemia.
we used a systems genetics approach to identify a co-regulated network of miRNAs that are associated with plasma LDL-C levels.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the microRNA regulatory network in the control of lipid metabolism.
the genetic architecture of dyslipidemia in mice.
identifying genetic and molecular mechanisms underlying dyslipidemia using a systems genetics approach.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

we identified a module of miRNas associated with circulating LDL cholesterol in a mouse model of dyslipidemia and we identified a small group of miRNAs that might have a coordinated effect on lipid metabolism.
the present findings suggest that miR-181a-5p, miR-199-5p, and miR21-5p may play a role in lipid homeostasis.
this study demonstrates that a high-fat diet (HFD) robustly rewires liver miRNA regulatory network.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified a co-regulated set of miRNAs that could be important for the control of plasma LDL-C in the liver.
we identified a set of miRNAs that are associated with plasma LDL-cholesterol levels in a murine model of dyslipidemia.
we identified a co-regulated miRNA module associated with circulating LDL-C levels in the DO mouse model of diet-induced dyslipidaemia.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a systems genetics approach can be successfully used to identify miRNA modules associated with lipid-related phenotypes in the liver, and that these miRNAs may be important targets in lipid-related metabolic disorders.
the DO population is well-suited to identify miRNA modules associated with complex traits, and that the DO population can provide a rich source of candidate miRNA biomarkers for human disease.
the use of a genetically diverse population, such as DO mice, provides a powerful approach to identify miRNA networks that may be relevant to dyslipidemia and other metabolic disorders.
